In the wider world they came under the patronage of Eithan Arelius, the eccentric and startlingly powerful head of the Arelius family, and Lindon took up soulsmithing while making a lasting enemy of the masked spear artist Jai Long. Guided by Eithan into the Blackflame Empire, Lindon learned the forbidden and destructive Path of Black Flame and bonded with Orthos, an embittered ancient tortoise who walks the same ruinous road. He defeated Jai Long in a decisive duel, dramatically raising his standing, but his open use of an outlawed power drew the attention of the empire's elite enforcers, the Skysworn, leaving him a far stronger but newly endangered figure as a larger crisis began to gather.

The consequences of Lindon's forbidden arts collide with a far larger emergency: a dreadgod, one of the titanic monsters whose awakenings devastate the world, is turning toward the Blackflame Empire. Rather than being simply punished for wielding outlawed Blackflame, Lindon and Yerin are drawn into service with the Skysworn, the empire's elite enforcers, as every available power is marshaled against the coming disaster. The approaching dreadgod, the Bleeding Phoenix, is a force beyond anything they have faced, drawing hordes of lesser dreadbeasts before it. For Yerin the threat is doubly dangerous, since her own blood-madra inheritance resonates uncomfortably with the Phoenix's blood-related power. Lindon throws himself into the empire's defense, aware that his hard-won strength is still small against a catastrophe of this scale.

As the Bleeding Phoenix nears, the empire's cities come under siege from waves of dreadbeasts, and Lindon, Yerin, Eithan, and the empire's forces fight to hold them. Lindon's strength grows under the pressure, but the crisis makes plain how far he still has to climb. The danger to Yerin sharpens: the closer the Bleeding Phoenix comes, the more her bound blood-madra presence stirs and strains against her control, threatening to turn her own inheritance against her. Emperor Naru Huan and the Naru family take direct part in the defense, and Eithan reveals more of his considerable power as the situation worsens. The defenders can hope only to endure and protect as many people as possible, since a dreadgod is not a thing that lesser artists can defeat outright.

The disaster reaches its peak as the Bleeding Phoenix itself descends on the empire, and the defenders are pushed to their limits simply to survive it and shield the people in its path. The specific danger to Yerin comes due: her bound blood-madra presence is drawn toward the Phoenix and torn from her, an event that gravely harms her and drives home how completely outmatched they all are against a dreadgod. Lindon, Eithan, Orthos, and the empire's greatest artists spend everything to blunt the catastrophe rather than to win against it. Amid the chaos of the Phoenix's assault, hidden things are stirred loose, and the fighting exposes secrets and dangers that had lain buried, setting up consequences that will reach well beyond the immediate battle.

By the book's close, the Bleeding Phoenix is driven off rather than destroyed, moving on and leaving the region battered and much of it in ruin, its people reeling from a catastrophe they could only endure. Yerin survives the loss of her bound blood-madra presence but is gravely weakened by it, and the ordeal makes unmistakably clear that Lindon and his companions need far greater power than they now possess. In the upheaval surrounding the dreadgod's attack, an ancient hidden place is opened, and Lindon is separated from the others and swept into it as the book ends. Having proven himself in the empire's defense, he is nonetheless carried off alone into an unknown ancient realm, cut off from Yerin and Eithan at the very moment they are all shaken by how small their strength remains. The book closes on that separation, with Lindon plunged into a new and isolating danger and the survivors left to reckon with the devastation.

characters.description: A teenager from the caverns of Detritus, the planet where the last remnant of humanity shelters underground while alien Krell raiders attack from above. Her father was a fighter pilot shot down during the defense of Alta Base when she was small, and the Defiant Defense Force recorded him as a coward who fled the battle, a verdict that cost his family its standing and left Spensa, her mother and her grandmother scraping a living outside the main cavern. Fierce, boastful and stubborn, raised on her grandmother's stories of Earth warriors, she wants nothing except to fly and to prove the accusation against her father false.
characters.name: Spensa Nightshade

characters.description: Spensa's father, a fighter pilot of the Defiant Defense Force known by the callsign Chaser. He was shot down during the Battle of Alta when Spensa was a young child, and the official record says he broke and ran from the fight. Spensa remembers a man who talked to her about the stars and refuses to accept that account of him.
characters.name: Zeen Nightshade

characters.description: Spensa's blind grandmother, who keeps the old stories alive: the voyage of the fleet that stranded their ancestors on Detritus, and the tales of Earth heroes she recites from memory. She tells Spensa to listen for the stars, an instruction Spensa takes as a figure of speech.
characters.name: Gran-Gran

characters.description: Spensa's closest friend from the caverns, careful and analytical where she is reckless, and far better than she is at the technical parts of the pilot's entrance exam. He would rather be safe than heroic, and he has a real gift for machinery.
characters.name: Rodge McCaffrey

characters.description: Admiral of the Defiant Defense Force, a hard veteran who flew at the Battle of Alta. She decides who is allowed into pilot training and is openly determined that the daughter of a man recorded as a deserter will never fly for the DDF.
characters.name: Ironsides

characters.description: The instructor assigned to train Skyward Flight, a retired pilot with a bad leg and a sour manner. He flew in the same flight as Spensa's father and is one of the few people who will speak of him at all. He insists on the DDF's own rule that any candidate who passes the entrance exam must be trained.
characters.name: Cobb

characters.description: The cadet appointed flightleader of Skyward Flight, from one of the most privileged families on Detritus; his mother sits on the National Assembly. Formal, rule-bound and irritatingly correct, he and Spensa dislike each other immediately, and she refuses to call him anything but Jerkface.
characters.name: Jorgen Weight

characters.description: A cadet from the farming caverns with a gentle, folksy manner and a habit of quoting the sayings of a saint. She is the best natural shot in the flight and by some distance the least aggressive person in it.
characters.name: Kimmalyn

characters.description: A cadet from a comfortable family who reads widely and questions both the DDF's chain of command and the assumptions Detritus society makes about rank and birth. She is usually the calmest voice in the flight.
characters.name: FM

characters.description: A cadet with a scholarly streak and a taste for long words, steady in the cockpit and quietly convinced that he should have been made flightleader instead of Jorgen.
characters.name: Arturo Mendez

characters.description: A brash, funny cadet who becomes Spensa's closest friend inside the flight. She is as hungry for glory as Spensa is and even less inclined to hold anything back.
characters.name: Hurl

characters.description: A large, cheerful cadet from a well-off family whose older brothers flew for the DDF before him. Very little troubles him.
characters.name: Nedd

characters.description: An enthusiastic, talkative cadet who loves stories about flying and is delighted simply to be allowed near a cockpit.
characters.name: Bim

characters.description: A short, strong cadet from a distant cavern community, who says little and whose accent the rest of the flight struggles with.
characters.name: Morningtide

characters.description: An artificial intelligence aboard a wrecked starfighter that Spensa finds buried in a cavern outside Alta. The ship is far more advanced than anything the DDF can build. Its last order from a pilot long dead was to hide and remain hidden, and it insists at length that it is not truly sentient while displaying curiosity, vanity, and a consuming interest in cataloguing mushrooms.
characters.name: M-Bot

characters.description: A small yellow slug from the caverns that repeats sounds it hears, fluting them back. It attaches itself to Spensa and cannot be persuaded to leave.
characters.name: Doomslug

recaps.ending: The Krell throw everything they have at Alta, including a lifebuster bomb meant to destroy the base and the caverns beneath it. The battle costs the DDF badly and kills several of Spensa's friends, Hurl among them. Flying M-Bot, Spensa deliberately uses her cytonic ability for the first time, teleports the ship, and gets above the debris field, where she finds the truth: the Krell fighters are unmanned drones controlled from an orbiting command ship crewed by living aliens. Humanity has not been hunted, it has been imprisoned and culled whenever it grew too numerous or too capable. Spensa destroys the command ship and the assault collapses. Ironsides gives up command and Cobb is made admiral of the DDF; Spensa's father is publicly cleared of cowardice, and Spensa is confirmed as a full pilot under the callsign Spin. M-Bot survives but is severely damaged and must be rebuilt. The DDF now knows the shape of its enemy for the first time, an alien civilization with vastly better technology that treats humans as a contained infestation, and it knows that Spensa can partly do what that civilization does. The ancient orbital platforms overhead, the origin of the fleet that stranded humanity here, and the identity of the people behind the drones are all left open, and Spensa's ability marks her as both the DDF's greatest asset and the thing its jailers will most want to stop.
recaps.in_short: The last of humanity lives in caverns on the planet Detritus, penned beneath a shell of orbiting debris and raided constantly by alien Krell fighters. Spensa Nightshade wants to be a pilot, but her father was shot down at the Battle of Alta and branded a coward, and Admiral Ironsides is determined to keep his daughter out of a cockpit. Forced into training by an old instructor's insistence on the rules, Spensa flies with Skyward Flight while secretly rebuilding a wrecked, far more advanced starfighter she finds in a cave, whose artificial intelligence calls itself M-Bot. Cadets die around her. She learns her father was not a coward: he was cytonic, able to hear the stars, and Ironsides shot him down out of fear of what that does to a pilot. When the Krell attack Alta with a weapon meant to end humanity on Detritus, Spensa uses the same ability herself, discovers that the Krell fighters are drones flown by aliens who have kept humanity imprisoned, and destroys their command ship.

recaps.text: The survivors of humanity live in caverns beneath the surface of the planet Detritus, sheltering under a shell of ancient orbiting debris while alien Krell ships raid from above. Their military, the Defiant Defense Force, treats fighter pilots as the highest calling there is. Spensa Nightshade has wanted to fly since she was small, but her father was shot down at the Battle of Alta and recorded as a coward who fled, and the label has followed his family ever since. Living outside the main cavern with her mother and her storytelling grandmother, Spensa studies for the pilot's entrance exam alongside her friend Rodge and passes it. Admiral Ironsides, who intends that no child of a deserter will ever fly, blocks her admission; the cadet instructor Cobb, who flew with her father, forces the issue by citing the DDF's own rule that anyone who passes must be trained. Spensa joins Skyward Flight under Cobb, where her fellow cadets include the strictly correct flightleader Jorgen, the sharpshooter Kimmalyn, the thoughtful FM, the wordy Arturo, the reckless Hurl, the easygoing Nedd, the talkative Bim and the taciturn Morningtide. Ironsides makes no secret of expecting Spensa to fail.

Cadet training is unforgiving. Cobb drills the flight in simulators and then sends them up in real fighters, and cadets are expected to fly against Krell raids while they are still learning. Rodge cannot face it and resigns from the flight, transferring to engineering, where he is far better suited. Refused a place in base housing because of her father's record, Spensa sleeps in a cave and hunts rats to eat. Exploring the caverns, she finds something extraordinary: a wrecked starfighter of a design nobody on Detritus builds, carrying an intact artificial intelligence that calls itself M-Bot. It insists it is not sentient, says its standing order is to remain hidden, and would rather she collected mushrooms. Spensa keeps the discovery to herself and begins scavenging parts to repair the ship, eventually bringing Rodge in to help with the electronics. Meanwhile the flight starts taking real losses, and Spensa's temper and her father's reputation keep her at odds with Jorgen and with the DDF's leadership.

Skyward Flight is thrown against Krell raids again and again, and the cadets begin to die. The survivors are drawn closer together, and Spensa's standing inside the flight rises even as her standing with command does not; Ironsides keeps looking for a reason to remove her. Work on M-Bot progresses slowly, the ship's systems being ancient and far beyond anything the DDF builds, with missing components the main obstacle. Spensa also begins to notice something she cannot explain, a sound like distant stars, strongest during combat, exactly the thing her grandmother has always told her to listen for. And she starts to suspect that the Krell do not fight like an enemy trying to win: their raids escalate and then break off, they strike some targets and ignore others, and nobody in the DDF can say what the Krell actually are.

The flight's losses mount, and the survivors carry them badly. The rivalry between Spensa and Jorgen erodes into something closer to respect as both are forced to lead under fire, and the flight itself becomes the thing Spensa is fighting for rather than her father's name alone. She keeps working on M-Bot, who grows steadily more talkative and more obviously a person than his own programming will admit he is. Piece by piece she learns more about her father's last flight, and the accounts she is given do not fit together; Cobb clearly knows more than he is willing to say. The sound she hears grows clearer, and she discovers that other pilots have heard it too, and that the DDF regards those pilots with fear rather than interest.

Spensa learns that the DDF has a secret category for pilots who hear what she hears. They are called defects, the leadership believes they become a danger to their own side, and her father was one of them. The knowledge explains why Ironsides fought so hard to keep her out of a cockpit, and it puts Spensa's own place in the DDF at risk, since discovery would end her career or worse. M-Bot, close to flightworthy again, becomes both her refuge and her secret, and hiding a working starfighter from her own military grows harder. The Krell attacks intensify, and the DDF cannot replace lost ships and lost pilots at the rate it is losing them. Skyward Flight, which began as a full class of cadets, is down to a fraction of its number.

The truth about the Battle of Alta finally reaches Spensa: her father did not flee. He heard the stars, something happened to him in the middle of the battle, and Ironsides shot him down herself, after which the DDF recorded it as cowardice. Spensa's fury at the admiral is complicated by the discovery that the danger Ironsides feared was not invented. Spensa's own connection to whatever lies beyond the debris field deepens, and she begins to understand that the enemy can hear her when she reaches for it. M-Bot flies again, unarmed but faster and more capable than anything in the DDF's inventory. Casualties among the cadets continue, and the DDF's hold on Alta becomes precarious as the Krell mass for something far larger than a raid.

The Krell launch an all-out assault on Alta carrying a lifebuster, a bomb capable of destroying the base and the caverns beneath it. Every pilot the DDF has goes up, and the flight suffers terribly; Hurl is among the dead. Spensa takes M-Bot into the battle, and in the middle of it she finally uses what she has been hearing, reaching out with her mind to teleport the ship above the debris field. There she finds the truth. The Krell fighters are drones, flown remotely by living aliens from a command ship in orbit, and those aliens have kept humanity penned on Detritus deliberately, bombing the population whenever it grew too numerous or too advanced. Spensa destroys the command ship and the assault collapses. Ironsides surrenders command and Cobb becomes admiral; Spensa's father is cleared, and Spensa is confirmed as a pilot with the callsign Spin. M-Bot survives, badly damaged. Humanity now knows it is a prisoner rather than a hunted remnant, that its jailers belong to a galactic civilization far beyond it technologically, and that at least one human can hear, and travel, the way they do.

characters.description: The book's author, who appears in the opening chapter in his own voice. He describes his decades-long struggle to write a book about the firebombing of Dresden, which he survived as an American prisoner of war, and the difficulty of putting such a massacre into words. He recounts visiting an old army friend, promising the friend's wife that the book will not glorify war, and deciding to tell the story through an invented figure, Billy Pilgrim. He notes that he was himself present at some of the events described.
characters.name: The narrator

characters.description: An ungainly, passive man from the fictional city of Ilium, New York, who becomes a prosperous optometrist after the war. As a young, untrained chaplain's assistant he was sent to Europe in World War II and captured during a German offensive, ending up as a prisoner in Dresden. He claims to have become unstuck in time, experiencing the moments of his life out of order, and to have been abducted by aliens. Whether this is genuine or a symptom of his wartime trauma is left open.
characters.name: Billy Pilgrim

characters.description: Billy's wife, the daughter of the wealthy owner of the optometry school Billy attends. Overweight, good-natured, and devoted to Billy, she is overjoyed to have married him and provides him with a comfortable, prosperous home life after the war.
characters.name: Valencia Merble Pilgrim

characters.description: A young American soldier captured alongside Billy behind enemy lines. Stupid, cruel, and full of violent war fantasies, he imagines himself the hero of a valiant trio and both keeps the helpless Billy moving and abuses him, blaming Billy for the group being cut off and captured.
characters.name: Roland Weary

characters.description: A sickly, vicious American prisoner obsessed with revenge, who collects grudges and promises to repay every wrong done to him. When Roland Weary dies as a prisoner and blames Billy for his death, Lazzaro swears that he will one day have Billy killed for it.
characters.name: Paul Lazzaro

characters.description: An alien species from the planet Tralfamadore who, in Billy's account, abduct him and put him on display in a zoo. They perceive time in four dimensions, seeing all moments of past, present, and future as permanently existing at once, so that death is merely one unpleasant moment among many. Their calm acceptance of fate, summed up in the refrain so it goes, shapes the way Billy comes to view his own life.
characters.name: The Tralfamadorians

characters.description: A young film actress whom, in Billy's account, the Tralfamadorians abduct and place in the zoo enclosure with him as a mate. She and Billy come to live together contentedly on display, and she grows to trust him.
characters.name: Montana Wildhack

characters.description: A middle-aged former high school teacher who volunteered for military service despite his age and is among the American prisoners held in Dresden. Decent, steady, and physically fit, he is chosen by the other captives as their leader.
characters.name: Edgar Derby

characters.description: A largely unknown and commercially unsuccessful science fiction writer whose strange novels Billy has long read and admired. Billy eventually meets him in person in Ilium and finds him working as the manager of a crew of newspaper delivery boys. Bitter and eccentric, Trout is astonished to discover that he has a devoted reader.
characters.name: Kilgore Trout

recaps.ending: The novel's threads converge on Billy Pilgrim's later years and the aftermath of Dresden. Billy's wife Valencia dies of carbon monoxide poisoning in a car while rushing to reach him after his plane crashes, leaving him the crash's sole survivor. Recovering in the hospital, he meets a historian researching the Dresden bombing. Billy goes public with his belief in the Tralfamadorians and their view of time, telling his story on the radio, and he claims already to know the moment of his own death: he will be shot years later by an assassin acting for the vengeful Paul Lazzaro. The book's wartime storyline ends just after the firebombing, with the prisoners digging corpses from the rubble. The kindly schoolteacher Edgar Derby is caught with a looted teapot and executed by firing squad. Then the war in Europe ends, the German guards vanish, and the surviving prisoners step out into a quiet, ruined springtime. The narrative closes on the sound of a bird's song, the only answer the book offers to the massacre.
recaps.in_short: The novel tells the story of Billy Pilgrim, an unremarkable American optometrist who survived the firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war and who believes he has become unstuck in time, living the events of his life out of sequence. The book opens with the author describing his own decades-long effort to write about the massacre he witnessed. It then follows Billy as he ricochets between his youth, his wartime capture during a German offensive, his abduction by aliens called Tralfamadorians who see all of time at once, his prosperous postwar life, and the destruction of Dresden, where he and other prisoners survived in a meat locker beneath a slaughterhouse. Along the way the vengeful Paul Lazzaro vows to have Billy killed, and the decent teacher Edgar Derby is executed for taking a teapot from the ruins. Through Billy's fatalistic, Tralfamadorian outlook, summed up by the phrase so it goes, the novel treats war, death, and free will as things simply to be endured.

recaps.text: In the opening chapter the author speaks in his own voice about his long struggle to write a book about the firebombing of Dresden in World War II, which he witnessed as an American prisoner of war, and about the difficulty of describing such a massacre. The story then turns to Billy Pilgrim, a mild optometrist from Ilium, New York, who claims to have come unstuck in time and to live the events of his life in scrambled order. The reader jumps with him between his comfortable postwar existence, his abduction by aliens, and his experiences as a young chaplain's assistant in the war. Untrained and unfit for combat, Billy is lost behind enemy lines during a German offensive in the company of Roland Weary, a brutal, fantasy-driven soldier who alternately drags him along and torments him. The two are soon captured by German troops, and Weary bitterly blames Billy for their plight.

As the prisoners are marched and shipped by boxcar deeper into Germany, Roland Weary dies of an infected wound, still cursing Billy; another prisoner, the vengeful Paul Lazzaro, swears he will one day have Billy killed for it. Meanwhile, in the time-scrambled narration, Billy describes being taken to the planet Tralfamadore and exhibited in an alien zoo. The Tralfamadorians see all of time at once and regard death with detachment, an outlook captured in the phrase so it goes. The captured Americans reach a prison camp where cheerful British officers have long been held, then are sent onward by train to Dresden, a beautiful, seemingly untouched city that is not yet a military target. Among Billy's fellow prisoners is Edgar Derby, a decent middle-aged teacher who volunteered for the war. The Americans are housed in a disused slaughterhouse numbered five.

The narration keeps leaping across Billy's life: his survival as the sole passenger of a later plane crash, his postwar optometry career, and his eventual meeting with the obscure science fiction writer Kilgore Trout, whose books he has long admired. In Dresden, the American prisoners work in a syrup factory and are visited by Howard Campbell, an American who has become a Nazi propagandist and tries to recruit them. Then the firebombing comes: overnight, Allied aircraft destroy the entire city in a firestorm while Billy and the others survive by sheltering in a deep meat locker beneath the slaughterhouse. When they climb out, Dresden has been reduced to a lifeless expanse of rubble and ash.

The narration gathers Billy's later life together. His wife Valencia dies of accidental carbon monoxide poisoning while racing to the hospital after his plane crash, and while recovering there Billy meets a historian writing about the Dresden raid. Billy travels to New York, goes on a radio program, and publicly tells the story of Tralfamadore and of seeing his own future, convinced that he will eventually be murdered by an aging Paul Lazzaro making good on his vow. In the war's final stretch, after the bombing, the prisoners are put to work digging bodies out of the ruins of Dresden. Edgar Derby, the steady schoolteacher, is arrested for taking a teapot from the wreckage and is executed by a German firing squad for looting. Soon afterward the war in Europe ends, the guards disappear, and Billy and the others walk out into a silent spring, where a bird calls out.
